_README: The turnloop migration's remaining tokio surface (docs/turnloop/p8-report.md).
`edges` and `lockfile` are GATED by scripts/tokio_inventory.py, strictly and in
both directions: a NEW edge fails, and a STALE entry fails too — so a lane that
removes an edge must delete its own line, and this file can never describe a tree
that is gone. Regenerate with `python3 scripts/tokio_inventory.py --update`, which
Per edge, the four hand-written fields are the ones `cargo tree` cannot give:
surface       what JS reaches it, or 'none' if no JS surface does
reached_when  the condition under which a program actually takes it
blocker       what has to exist before it can move
plan          its group in the report's costed removal plan; every edge is in
exactly one group, and `--list` prints the totals
Group J is not in the costed plan: it is the four database wrappers, which are
being DELETED rather than migrated because each wraps a pure-JS npm package that
Perry can now compile from source. Their edges leave with the crates.
`source_sites` is NOT gated: a comment naming tokio::spawn moves it, so a failure
there would carry no information. It is recorded because it is the only number
that says how much code sits behind an edge.

edges.surface: none. The separate `perry-compose` binary (a Docker-Compose-like driver for Apple Container / Podman). perry-stdlib reaches it only under the non-default `container` feature, which `full` does not enable.
edges.reached_when: running `perry-compose`, or a build that explicitly enables `perry-stdlib/container`
edges.blocker: async end-to-end across ~14.8k lines (`async-trait` backends, `tokio::process::Command`, `tokio::time::timeout`). A rewrite of a non-JS tool; no event-loop transport is involved.

edges.surface: `http.createServer()` / `https.createServer()` on a declining path, `http2.createServer` / `createSecureServer` on a declining path, the SCHED_RR cluster worker's fd-inject loop, and the raw-`'upgrade'` peeler
edges.reached_when: a thread that does not own its agent's loop -- since turnloop P9 that is a second thread acting for an agent another thread already owns (a host pump thread; Android's UI thread for `perry-native`), not a worker agent -- or a host where Loop::new failed; also a SCHED_RR cluster worker, which is Node's non-Windows DEFAULT policy. NO LONGER a SO_REUSEPORT cluster worker, and no longer a server with `new WebSocketServer({ server })` attached at listen time.
edges.blocker: No missing turnloop capability is left; what remains is the deletion itself, sequenced behind #11084. Both halves of the old blocker are closed. (1) The P1 coexistence rule: a thread that does not own its agent's loop posts its work to the thread that does (`perry_ffi::agent_post`, turnloop P10) -- both serve the same JS heap. perry-ext-net does exactly that for every socket, listener, TLS session and deadline since it dropped tokio (`turnloop_io::on_loop`), which is the worked example for this crate: route a declined thread's `listen()` to the owner's `try_listen_on_turnloop` instead of building a hyper accept loop. The one decline posting cannot serve, a host where Loop::new failed, reports ENOTSUP there rather than keeping a second event loop. (2) The SCHED_RR fd-inject premise ('turnloop's Driver has no API that adopts a foreign fd') was stale: turnloop has had `Driver::attach(Detached)` since alpha.6 and `Detached::from_fd` / `from_listener_fd` (alpha.8, turnloop#108), and perry-runtime now exposes it to bindings as `turnloop_net::adopt_stream` (C ABI `js_perry_net_adopt_stream`, perry-ffi `turnloop_net::adopt_stream`), which puts a connected stream fd/SOCKET on the agent's loop under a binding-chosen id -- exactly what `spawn_rr_inject_loop`'s descriptors from `cluster_bind::recv_fd` need, once `turnloop_serve` can take a connection it did not accept itself. What is left: delete the hyper HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 accept loops (`server.rs`'s `serve_http_connection` + `spawn_rr_inject_loop`, `https_server.rs`, `http2_server.rs`), the raw-'upgrade' peeler (`raw_upgrade.rs`, `upgrade.rs` -- #11084 is rewriting both on the hyper path right now, which is why this lane did not touch them), and feed the RR descriptors through `adopt_stream` into turnloop_serve. CLOSED earlier: the SO_REUSEPORT half (alpha.6 `ReusePort::Share`) and the attached `WebSocketServer` (docs/turnloop/ws-report.md).
edges.issue: unfiled -- P8; perry#10395 (the posting route) is the pattern

edges.reached_when: as `hyper` above: a thread that does not own its agent's loop, or a host where Loop::new failed
edges.blocker: goes with hyper: the `server-auto` connection builder and `TokioIo`. No blocker of its own; see the `hyper` row.

edges.reached_when: NO LONGER always. `client_turnloop::try_dispatch` is offered every exchange before `dispatch_request` and takes cleartext `http://` requests with no body, no explicit Agent, no per-request timeout, no proxy and none of the three bypass headers; reqwest gets everything it declines. So: `https://`, any request body, an explicit `http.Agent`, `options.timeout`/`req.setTimeout`, `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`, a URL with credentials, the CONNECT/TRACE/TRACK methods, and `TE: trailers` / `Connection: Upgrade` / `Expect: 100-continue` (which keep their own raw-socket bypasses).
edges.blocker: The decline set above, shrinking per lane: TLS (`perry-tls-session` above the same handle, as `perry-ext-ws`'s client does), request-body framing plus `Lifecycle` deadlines armed on `tl::timer_arm`, keep-alive via `turnloop_http::client::Pool`, and the Agent lane. CORRECTION to the older note: `agent.rs` is NOT a duplicate of reqwest's pool and is not the blocker it was described as. It is a real per-origin admission engine (FIFO waiter queue, maxSockets/maxTotalSockets/maxFreeSockets, socket facades) that sits ABOVE the transport and survives the migration nearly intact; the reqwest coupling there is 9 call sites in `client_for_agent`/`client_for_agent_tls`/`agent_pool_config`. Also stale in that note: the three raw `tokio::net::TcpStream` bypasses are `plain_client.rs` (`TE: trailers`), `continue_client.rs` (`Expect: 100-continue`) and `client_upgrade.rs` (`Connection: Upgrade`, #10468) — NOT the `agent.createConnection` override, which reaches no tokio at all (it runs on perry-ext-net's raw_net vtable in `client_connect_override.rs`). `Http1Connection` hands `Event::Trailers`, `Event::Informational` and `Event::Upgrade` back to the caller, so all three ARE deletable by this migration. `createConnection` is a different problem: it needs an fd-adoption ABI that does not exist yet — `turnloop::Detached::from_fd` + `Loop::attach` are real, but neither `perry_ffi::turnloop_net` nor `perry-runtime`'s `turnloop_net/abi.rs` exposes them to a binding crate.
edges.issue: #10328 (the agent cache never evicts); the transport is unfiled — P6 named it, P8 confirms it

edges.surface: every row above, plus the three raw-TcpStream client bypasses. NO LONGER `http2.connect`: the HTTP/2 client is turnloop-only now (the `h2` row is gone), and `node:http2` reaches no tokio of its own.
edges.reached_when: always (the node:http client) or a thread that could not get a loop of its own — since turnloop P9 that is a second thread acting for an agent another thread already owns (a host pump thread; Android's UI thread for `perry-native`), not a worker agent, or a host where Loop::new failed (the server)
edges.blocker: the union of the rows above, and NOT group D's own work -- the plan's row D already said so (“its last, once C and E are done”). E is done and D's `h2` half is done; what is left is `reqwest` + `tokio-rustls` (plan C, the node:http/https CLIENT: ~1,950 lines of `agent.rs` plus three raw `tokio::net::TcpStream` bypasses) and `hyper` + `hyper-util` (plan A, the declining HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 SERVER accept loops plus the SCHED_RR fd-inject loop -- plan A's perry-ext-net half is done, and its `adopt_upgraded_tcp_stream` now takes a `std::net::TcpStream`, so no tokio type crosses into perry-ext-net any more). `node:http2`'s CLIENT reaches no tokio at all now -- `http2_server/session.rs` contains no `tokio::` code -- so this edge is held open entirely by A and C. Note for whoever closes A: deleting the hyper accept loops removes every I/O-DRIVING tokio use but NOT tokio's type vocabulary, which is baked into structs both transports build (`ServerResponse::{response_tx, stream_tx, stream_in_flight, connection_close}`, `HttpServer::{shutdown_tx, request_rx, upgrade_rx}`, `Http2StreamHandle::response_tx`, `ShapeBody::Stream`) and kept alive by the shared dispatchers that branch `match turnloop { Some / None }`. That is a separable second step.

edges.reached_when: a host where `Loop::new` failed — the only remaining case now that the `tokio-wait-driver` A/B arm has been deleted. **The agent-shaped decline is CLOSED** (turnloop P10, perry#10395 step 2): a second thread acting for an agent another thread already owns — a host pump thread, Android's UI thread for `perry-native` — now hands its work to that owner through `perry_ffi::agent_post` instead of keeping this driver alive for itself. No longer a worker agent (P9 gave every agent a loop), and no longer TLS (`rediss://`, the default since `REDIS_TLS` defaults to true, is carried by turnloop).
edges.blocker: SUPERSEDED BY A SCOPE DECISION (Ralph, 2026-09-17): this crate is going away, so this edge goes with it and NOBODY SHOULD CONVERT IT. `ioredis` is a pure-JS npm package, and the native wrapper exists only because Perry was TypeScript-only at one time. The plan is to delete the wrapper and compile the package from its own JS source, which removes this edge by deletion rather than by migration. Do not spend a lane on a turnloop transport here. The pre-existing blocker, kept for the record and no longer actionable: two reasons left, and neither is specific to redis or to this binding — both are an ABSENCE of a loop rather than a hole in the path. Only ONE reason is left now that the `tokio-wait-driver` A/B arm has been deleted: a host where `Loop::new` failed has no loop to post to. It is one shared decision, not four conversions — every plan-A and plan-B edge names that same single cause. Narrow third case, documented rather than fixed: `net_available()` CLAIMS a route without building a loop, so a client created in the window between the owner claiming its slot and publishing its `Poster` sees no route and is created on the legacy transport for its life. TLS is done: perry-db-turnloop installs a client session through perry-tls-turnloop.
edges.issue: #10335 — spawn_blocking/block_on CLOSED for the agent-shaped decline by #10395 step 2

edges.surface: `new MongoClient()` — connect, find, insert, update, delete, aggregate
edges.reached_when: a thread that could not get a loop of its own — since turnloop P9 that is a second thread acting for an agent another thread already owns (a host pump thread; Android's UI thread for `perry-native`), not a worker agent, or a host where Loop::new failed, plus `mongodb+srv://`, several hosts, `replicaSet=`, `compressors=`, a per-connection TLS key (`tlsCAFile`, `tlsInsecure`, …), an unparsable URI, or no /dev/urandom. A plain `tls=true`/`ssl=true` no longer declines.

edges.surface: every async stdlib surface: the `async-runtime` feature gates `common::async_bridge` and `perry_ffi_async`, i.e. the whole promise bridge and the `perry_ffi_spawn_blocking*` / `spawn_async` C ABI every perry-ext-* crate settles its promises through.
edges.reached_when: always — `full` implies it, and 20 other features imply it individually
edges.blocker: this is the hardest edge in the tree and it is NOT a separable layer: `async_bridge::RUNTIME` is tokio because its clients hand it tokio futures. Inside perry-stdlib NEITHER client named by the two previous revisions of this entry survives: group G deleted the reqwest fetch fallback (#11101) and group H moved TLS onto perry-tls-session's sans-I/O rustls session (#11102). What is left is the tokio SOCKETS under the bundled `node:tls` server, the `net` client and the `wss://` connector -- their TLS moved, their I/O did not. Every perry-ext-* driver also reaches the same runtime through the `perry_ffi_*` C seam, so the bridge's work did not go away with the drivers. It goes when the last of them goes, not before. P4's v1 shims (`spawn_blocking`, `spawn_blocking_with_reactor`, `spawn_async`) cannot move onto turnloop's bounded pool because their callers hold a thread for a CONNECTION's lifetime, not a job's (PerryTS/turnloop#42).

SYNC tungstenite on its own thread — not a tokio edge at all. #11065 bumped this crate's pin from 0.24 to 0.30, so the tree-wide tungstenite major-version split is gone: this edge now resolves to the same 0.30.0 as turnloop-websocket. `turnloop_websocket::Connection` works over a blocking `std::net::TcpStream` as happily as over anything else, so the migration off tungstenite entirely is still mechanical — but it cannot be built or run from the shared Linux box, and an unexecutable migration is not one to land blind.
